audio_caption: The audio clip starts with a male speaker announcing "Novara Media" and noting it's the eve of the election, and welcomes another man. A second male speaker jokingly identifies himself as Owen Jones. The first male speaker then asks him what he's been up to, using a casual term. The second male speaker then replies that they've been out in Croydon, "pounding those streets," knocking on doors, and that they had an "absolute army" and it was "phenomenal."

The audio starts with a male speaker noting a 150-vote majority, for Gavin Barwell. He mentions that the Tories "have an excellent record on housing," claiming too many affordable homes are built. He then describes a large, young and diverse "army," contrasting it with those "on the sharp end" of Barwell's policies who struggle with private rents. Next, the speaker proudly says they "swept through the constituency," claiming that "the Tories have the money" and "we have the people on the ground."

The audio clip starts with a male speaker discussing a "racket of vested interests" and mentioning receiving a flyer from a volunteer. Another male speaker expresses skepticism about this volunteer's status. The first speaker then describes the size and reach of their support network across the country, admitting to feeling "burnt out" from campaigning, but notes the encouraging aspect of encountering first-time door-knockers. Throughout the clip, an ambient sound of general chatter and distant traffic noises create the backdrop for the conversation.

The audio clip features an interview-style conversation. A male interviewer prompts the subject, a male speaker, to elaborate on his feelings about the campaign. The speaker acknowledges past doubts but expresses pleasant surprise. He mentions that, while his previous concern was that people had already made up their minds and were not willing to listen, the campaign has proven him wrong.  Sounds of general conversations can be heard consistently in the background.

The audio clip features two male speakers in an outdoor setting, indicated by background noise and other speech. The first speaker is reflecting on how he was "proved decisively wrong", explaining that his initial fears were that they would get very low polling numbers, but has since been inspired because "lots of people have just changed their minds." The second man chimes in stating "people are more up for socialism than we thought." There is a brief interjection with another male voice before the first speaker closes with "I want a bit of clairvoyance, right?"

The clip begins with an ambient sound environment suggesting an outdoor setting, filled with various indistinguishable sounds.  A single male speaker then begins speaking, addressing an audience anticipating an election, asking for predictions of specific newspaper headlines, naming "The Sun," "The Daily Mail," and his own paper, "The Guardian."

The audio begins with two male speakers discussing potential newspaper headlines. One predicts that "Corbyn will nationalize your mother" and rename people as "Osama Bin Laden", then the other speaker hypothesizes that the Daily Mail will require street names to change to "Vladimir Lenin is welcome", and for everyone to "wear Soviet berets". In the background, speech and ambient sounds suggest a public environment.

The audio clip begins with speech from a male speaker referring to "The Guardian". He discusses the newspaper's perceived bias, clarifying that it's liberal but not socialist, naming left-leaning figures like "me and George Monbiot". The speaker has a conversational tone. His words are punctuated by indistinct background chatter, suggesting a public space setting.

The clip begins with a male speaker passionately stating, "I mean, the Guardian came up with the 'Ned story' which was wholeheartedly about Labour in this election." He continues expressing uncertainty and then enthusiastically says, "Yeah, vote Labour!" Another male speaker responds, mentioning the neck-and-neck state in the polls, and asks what will happen. The first male speaker replies and hopes Labour will do something good. A final male speaker announces the recording is going out on election day. Throughout the clip, there is background noise suggesting an outdoor or public environment.

The clip begins with one male speaker, who is enthusiastic. He describes a desire to seize an opportunity with someone named "Owen Jones". He requests that the camera focus on a person delivering a "motivational speech." He poses questions to the speaker about what actions people should take that afternoon to achieve a socialist government. He pleads for people to make calls and "do the best we can". Another male voice answers, pleading with the listener to look at his "puppy dog" eyes. He says "seriously" and "genuinely serious here." The second male speaker implores listeners to do "every last thing you can do" at this moment to get people out to vote for Labour, asking "then when?" The sound of people talking in the background is faintly audible.

The audio begins with a male speaker, with a calm and persuasive tone. He promotes the Labour party's vision, emphasizing their ability to build houses, create jobs, overcome poverty, and avoid burdening young people with debt. He urges listeners to vote and to bring others to the polling station, referencing the encouragement from favorable polling data. He also cites the support from younger voters, non-voters, and women. A brief musical interlude follows, but the clip abruptly cuts off.

The audio begins with ambient sounds suggesting an outdoor gathering or public place, characterized by general background chatter and indistinct voices. A male speaker with a passionate tone begins talking about encouraging young people to vote, suggesting they are perceived as lazy and don't care. He urges listeners to text, WhatsApp, or use any means to convey the importance of voting as a big opportunity for genuine change. He encourages voters to influence their grandparents by discussing the "dementia tax", the "scrapping of the triple lock", and other issues. He emphasizes that they can turn the tide by encouraging everyone they know to vote. The male speaker transitions to "Thank you and it's a pleasure to share this historic moment with you". Another male speaker follows. The clip may be shared on Facebook.

The audio begins with a male speaker suggesting to "message 20 people who you haven't talked about politics for in the last year," and to canvass if able. Another male speaker takes over to say "it's so easy," that people will be paired with experienced volunteers, and that it makes a difference and will "change the world." The first speaker returns to add that you don't need to be a policy expert, but to simply explain why you are voting Labour, before suggesting "voting is Friday if you vote Conservative." Both speakers have a conversational tone. There is ambient sound in the background, though the nature is not clear from the audio.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker encouraging listeners to relax and watch news coverage of a certain ideology. The speaker is calm and sounds like he is recording a promotional segment. Following the end of the speech is a musical tone.
